name: May-Thurner Syndrome

criteria.description: Compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery demonstrated by imaging
Presence of left lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) without other obvious cause
Clinical signs of venous stasis such as unilateral leg swelling, pain, or venous claudication

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Imaging evidence of left iliac vein compression plus clinical symptoms consistent with venous obstruction; presence of left-sided DVT supports diagnosis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis often requires combination of clinical presentation and imaging modalities such as venography, CT venography, or intravascular ultrasound

pathognomonic.notes: Identified via imaging; hallmark of syndrome

pathognomonic.symptomName: Left lower extremity deep vein thrombosis
searchTerms: blood clot in left leg vein
pain or heaviness in left leg

common.notes: Pain on exertion relieved by rest

common.symptomName: Visible superficial varicosities on left leg
searchTerms: visible varicose veins on left leg

occasional.symptomName: Left lower extremity skin discoloration or hyperpigmentation
searchTerms: brown patches on left leg skin

occasional.symptomName: Venous ulceration on left lower leg
occasional.notes: Late complication of chronic venous hypertension
searchTerms: open sore on left lower leg
venous leg ulcer on left leg

occasional.notes: May occur due to pelvic venous congestion
Secondary to nerve compression or venous congestion
searchTerms: numbness or pins and needles left leg

rare.symptomName: Pulmonary embolism secondary to left leg DVT
searchTerms: lung blood clot from leg DVT

rare.notes: Fibrotic skin changes from chronic venous insufficiency
searchTerms: long-term leg swelling with skin thickening
chronic swollen leg with skin changes

rare.symptomName: Left lower limb venous claudication mimicking arterial claudication
searchTerms: leg vein pain like artery pain
venous leg cramping mimicking artery pain
leg pain from veins resembling arterial claudication

laboratory: Normal coagulation profile unless thrombophilia present
imaging: Compression of left common iliac vein on CT venography or MR venography
Intravascular ultrasound showing venous spur or stenosis
Venography demonstrating collateral venous flow and obstruction
genetic: No specific genetic mutations identified; thrombophilia screening recommended
other: Physical exam showing unilateral leg swelling and varicosities
Venous duplex ultrasound may show left iliac vein obstruction

distinguishingFeatures: DVT can occur without iliac vein compression
No characteristic iliac vein spur or compression on imaging
Usually bilateral or not limited to left leg
No iliac vein compression on imaging
Compression occurs at different anatomical site

redFlags: Sudden onset of severe unilateral leg swelling and pain
Signs of pulmonary embolism such as dyspnea or chest pain
Progressive venous ulceration or skin necrosis
references: May R, Thurner J. The cause of the predominantly sinistral occurrence of thrombosis of the pelvic veins. Angiology. 1957.
O'Sullivan GJ, et al. May-Thurner syndrome: diagnosis and management. Cardiovasc Intervent Radiol. 2000.
Raju S, Neglén P. May-Thurner syndrome: update and review. Ann Vasc Surg. 2006.
